question_en: Which of the following best describes a management buyout?
option_b: Outside shareholders install new management
option_c: Private equity investors buy out management's shares
explanation_en: When investors (usually a group of investors) purchase a controlling share of a company and the company's shares are no longer publicly traded, the company has been taken private. When investors finance that share buyout with a large proportion of debt, it is referred to as a leveraged buyout (LBO). A management buyout (MBO) is a type of LBO in which members of a company's existing management team are part of the group buying out the other shareholders (Choices B and C). The MBO is usually undertaken to restructure the company, increase its value, and eventually take it public again.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best describes a characteristic of preference shares?
option_a: They cannot be callable or putable.
option_b: Their regular dividends are fixed at issuance.
option_c: They legally obligate the issuer to make regular dividend payments.
explanation_en: Companies often issue shares of common stock to raise capital. With callable (ie, redeemable) common shares, the issuing company (ie, issuer) reserves the right to buy back shares from investors at a predetermined call price. This call feature may limit potential upside on price appreciation for investors, so callable common shares offer high dividend payments in return to compensate for the risk. (Choice A) Call option allow investors to purchase shares of common stock at a predetermined price. (Choice C) Putable common shares allow investors to sell shares of common stock back to the issuer at a predetermined price.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: All else equal, a company's return on equity will most likely decrease if:
option_b: it issues large amounts of new common shares.
option_c: its net income increases at a faster rate than its book value of equity.
explanation_en: ROE is the rate of return that common shareholders receive on equity capital invested in a company. Issuing common shares increases the book value of equity, which leads to a decrease in ROE, all else equal. Since net income and book value of equity are accounting measures, ROE may sometimes be impacted by management's choice of a reporting method (eg, revenue recognition policies, depreciation assumptions). Analysts should consider differences in reporting methods when evaluating ROE across multiple firms. (Choice A) A change in a company's stock price leads to a change in the market value of equity, which has no direct impact on ROE since ROE is calculated using the book value, not the market value. (Choice C) Net income increasing faster than the book value of equity would lead to an increase, not a decrease, in ROE.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Investors' required rate of return on common shares is most likely used to estimate a company's:
option_b: return on equity.
option_c: book value of equity.
explanation_en: Investors must be compensated for bearing risk, so securities trade at prices such that expected returns reflect expected risks. Expected return is interpreted as the minimum return required by investors since a lower return would be less than fair compensation. This risk/return relationship applies to new issues of common stock as well as to existing shares. Investors' compensation for bearing risk is the issuer's cost of sharing that risk. Therefore, the investors' expected (ie, required) rate of return can be used as a proxy for the company's cost of equity. (Choice B) Return on equity (ROE) is an accounting return calculated as the ratio of net income to book value of shareholders' equity. Required rates of return are not used to estimate ROE. (Choice C) The book value of a company's equity is the book value of assets less the book value of liabilities. Required rates of return are not used to estimate the book value of a company's equity.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Voting rights attached to sponsored depository receipts most likely belong to:
option_b: the investor of the depository receipts.
option_c: the company that the depository receipts were issued for.
explanation_en: Depository receipts (DRs) allow investors access to foreign securities without having to transact directly in the foreign market. A depository receipt is created when a company transfers shares of its own stock into a bank in another country. The depository bank then helps make the DRs available to investors in the bank's country. Depository receipts can be sponsored or unsponsored. In the case of sponsored DRs, the company is directly involved in issuing its DRs. Sponsored DR investors have the same voting rights as common shareholders of the company's stock. For unsponsored DRs, the company is not involved in issuing the DRs. The depository bank retains the voting rights.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: The priorities that preferred shareholders have compared to common shareholders are least likely related to:
option_b: payment of dividends.
option_c: claim on assets upon liquidation.
explanation_en: Equity securities' characteristics Common Preferred Voting rights Some corporate actions (eg, M&A) and board seats Usually none Dividends Payable only after preferred Payable in full before common Assets Residual claim after all other obligations retired Priority claim over common for asset distributions There are two types of equity securities: common stocks and preferred stocks (ie, preference shares). Corporations must have common shares outstanding, which represent the ownership interests in the company. As owners, common stockholders: share in the company's operating performance, participate in its governance through voting rights, and have a residual claim on the company's assets in the case of liquidation. Companies may raise additional equity capital by issuing preferred stock. Unlike common stock, preferred shares normally carry no voting rights and do not participate in company operating performance. However, preferred shares rank ahead of (ie, have preference over) common shares, as preferred shareholders receive: preferred dividends, once declared, before any common stock dividends can be paid (Choice B), and shares' par value before common shareholders receive any distributions, upon liquidation (Choice C).

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: A group of investors use a large amount of debt financing to purchase all the shares of a company's publicly traded stock. The investors are most likely executing a:
option_b: venture capital transaction.
option_c: private investment in public equity.
explanation_en: A leveraged buyout (LBO) occurs when a group of investors purchases all the outstanding shares of a publicly traded company using a significant amount of debt. The purchase is not entirely financed by debt, as the investors also use equity capital to finance the purchase. An LBO is known as "taking the company private," since after the purchase, the investors have complete control over the company. Company insiders, such as management, often execute the LBO, in which case it may be referred to as a management buyout (MBO). The LBO is structured such that the funds are borrowed by the acquired company. Targets for LBOs often have high cash flow and/or undervalued assets, which can be used to pay down the transaction debt. The LBO investors often restructure the company, the goal being to sell the company in public markets at a price that constitutes a substantial annual return on the investors' original equity investment. (Choice B) Venture capital investment involves providing early-stage financing to companies with high growth potential that are in need of funds to expand the business. (Choice C) A private investment in public equity (PIPE) occurs when a publicly traded company has an urgent need for funds in a short time. The company sells its stock to a large, accredited investor at a discount to the stock's market value. The PIPE can be more efficient and less regulatorily burdensome than a public offering.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: When investing in nondomestic equities, an advantage of global registered shares over unsponsored depository receipts is most likely the:
option_b: receipt of 100% of dividend payouts.
option_c: reduced exposure to exchange rate risk.
explanation_en: Investing in nondomestic equities Security Issuer Quoted/traded Issuer's equity in Issuer's domestic Company domestic market currency Direct Exchange's local GRS Company currency ADR US depository USD Exchange's local GDR Local depository Indirect currency BLDR ETF holding Exchange's local (ETF) ADRs/GDRs currency ADR = American depository receipt GDR = Global depository receipt BLDR = Basket of listed depository receipts GRS = Global registered share ETF = Exchange-traded fund Investments in nondomestic equities can be made directly through global registered shares (GRSs) or indirectly through depository receipts (DRs). GRSs are identical shares issued in multiple countries; each share carries the same ownership interests (eg, dividends, voting rights) but is traded in a market's local currency. DRs, also traded in local currency, are interests in accounts at depositories that hold the foreign company shares. DRs may be sponsored or unsponsored. Returns on DRs match the performance of the shares in each account. However, the depository, not the investor, is the legal owner of the foreign company shares. Whereas investors in GRSs retain full voting rights, holders of unsponsored DRs may lack voting rights if the depository chooses to retain them. (Choice B) Investors in both GRSs and DRs receive 100% of the dividends. (Choice C) GRSs and DRs expose investors to the same currency risk. Both are traded in the local currency, avoiding the need to trade currencies to invest in nondomestic equities. However, since the value of a company is usually determined by the share price in its domestic market, currency fluctuations can affect the price of a GRS or DR.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: If a company's cost of equity differs from an equity investor's required rate of return, which of the following best explains that difference?
option_a: A company's future cash flows are uncertain and unknown
option_b: The company announces that it plans to undertake riskier projects
option_c: Cost of equity is calculated after tax since dividends are tax deductible
explanation_en: Investors must be compensated for bearing risk when providing capital to companies. Equity investors base their required rate of return on expected future cash flows. Since these are uncertain and unknown, different investors will have different estimates of the company's future cash flows. This leads to different investors having different required rates of return. Since companies seek to issue capital at the lowest potential cost, a company will issue equity capital at the lowest rate that will allow it to raise sufficient capital, which becomes the company's cost of equity. Investors with required rates of return less than or equal to this rate will purchase the company's securities; those that have higher required rates of return will not. For a given amount of equity issued, the company's cost of equity will be a single rate. Investors will have varied required rates of return, which often differ from a company's cost of equity. (Choice B) A company taking on riskier projects would most likely increase both its cost of equity and investors' required rate of return, assuming the investors would be aware of the projects. This is not a reason for differences between the cost of equity and investors' required rates of return. (Choice C) The company's cost of debt, not its cost of equity, is calculated after tax. Interest expense is a tax-deductible expense for the company, but dividends are not.

question_en: All else equal, if the actual return from investing in a company's stock is less than the investors' minimum required rate of return, which of the following is most likely to increase? The company's:
option_b: cost of equity.
option_c: return on equity.
explanation_en: Types of preference shares (preferred stock) Cumulative Accrues for past dividends that are unpaid Noncumulative Does not accrue dividends that are undeclared and unpaid in past periods Participating Allows for additional dividend payments if company profits exceed a certain threshold Nonparticipating Fixed dividend; no additional payments based on company performance Convertible Can convert into a specified number of common shares Callable Allows issuer to buy back shares from investors for a specified price Putable Allows investors to sell shares back to issuer for a specified price Preference (preferred) shares ownership represents a form of equity investment in a company. Preference shares may grant certain benefits such as dividends and, in some cases, conversion to common stock. Participating preference shares provide additional dividend payments to shareholders if the company's profits exceed a certain benchmark. Unlike participating preferred shares, nonparticipating preference shares do not provide such benefits. (Choice A) Voting is a right bestowed on common shareholders, not preferred shareholders. (Choice C) The provision to sell shares back to a company at a predetermined price is not a feature of participating preferred stock.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Participating preference shares allow preferred shareholders to:
option_a: vote in annual board of director elections.
option_b: receive additional dividends if profits exceed a threshold.
option_c: sell shares back to the company at a predetermined price.
explanation_en: Characteristics of common shares • Rank below preference shares in respect to ◦ Dividend payments ◦ Asset distribution during liquidation • Represent ownership stake in a company • Share in the operating performance of the company • Typically offer voting rights for shareholders to participate in decision-making process • Companies can choose to pay all, some, or none of their profits in dividends Common shares are a type of equity security that provides financing for the issuing company in exchange for a claim on the company's net assets. They are the predominant type of equity financing used by companies. Common shares represent an equity ownership stake, allowing the investor to share in the company's operating performance, vote on certain company decisions, and make claims on the company's net assets in the event of bankruptcy. The claims of common shareholders rank below debt holders and preference shareholders, adding to the risk of common shares. (Choice B) The proceeds from the sale of common shares are not loans, so there is no repayment obligation at maturity (ie, principal payment) as would be the case for bonds. Since common shares have no maturity, they may remain outstanding in perpetuity or until the company repurchases and retires them. (Choice C) Most common shares allow shareholders to participate in major corporate governance decisions (eg, mergers and acquisitions) by the company through voting. The company will specify how many votes each share receives.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: A depository receipt allows a local investor to invest in:
option_a: local securities through a foreign exchange.
option_b: foreign securities through a local exchange.
option_c: foreign securities through a foreign exchange.
explanation_en: American depository receipt (ADR) overview Rule 144A Level I Level II Level III Yes, but only QIB private Raise new US capital No No Yes, public offering placement Yes, more robust filing SEC registration None Yes, basic Yes, basic required Over-the- NYSE, NASDAQ, Trading venues Unlisted NYSE, NASDAQ, AMEX counter AMEX Listing fees Low Low High High Size/earnings None None Yes Yes requirements QIB = Qualified institutional buyers Foreign companies can access US investors and broaden their equity investor base by creating American depository receipts (ADR). In a sponsored ADR, a foreign company deposits shares of its stock with certain banks that create dollar-denominated certificates (ie, ADRs), which will usually be listed on an exchange. An ADR trades just like a stock and generally tracks the underlying value of the company's shares that trade on a foreign exchange. There are four primary types of ADR listings, each with progressively more stringent listing and corporate governance requirements: Rule 144A ADR: unregistered and privately sold only to qualified investors, with resale restrictions Level I: SEC-registered and trades over-the-counter (OTC) with basic access to US investors Level II: SEC-registered and exchange-traded with better investor access but higher cost and more requirements Level III: most stringent SEC registration requirements; can be used by foreign-listed firms to raise new equity capital and for acquisitions (Choices B and C) Level I ADRs give foreign-listed firms the most basic access to US markets and investors. SEC filing requirements are less stringent, and these ADRs may not be sold to raise new equity capital in the US.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following statements best describes a feature of callable common shares? Callable common shares give:
option_a: investors the right to purchase shares of common stock.
option_b: issuers the right to buy back shares of common stock from investors.
option_c: investors the right to sell shares of common stock back to the issuer.
explanation_en: Characteristics of preference shares (preferred stock) • Rank above common shares in respect to ◦ Dividend payments ◦ Asset distribution during liquidation • Do not generally offer voting rights • Can be callable, putable, or convertible • Dividends are ◦ Not contractual obligations ◦ Generally fixed at issuance Preference shares are a type of equity security that provides financing for the issuing company. Preference shareholders receive a regular dividend payment from the company that is fixed at issuance. Like dividends on common shares, preferred dividends are not contractual obligations, and missing payments will not send a company into default. Preference shares rank above common shares when dividends and claims on a company's net assets are paid during liquidation. In that situation, preference shareholders must receive their dividends before common shareholders can receive theirs. This requirement is taken a step further in regard to cumulative preference shares: A company must pay any current and previously unpaid dividends to cumulative preference shareholders before common dividends can be paid. (Choice A) Unlike common shares, preference shares usually do not provide voting rights to the shareholders. When exceptions occur, preference shareholders are typically allowed to vote on only those matters relevant to their shares. (Choice B) Dividends on preference shares are fixed and generally larger than those on common shares. This helps to make preference shares more attractive to potential investors, despite lacking the upside potential of common shares.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: A foreign company is considering listing its shares on a US exchange as an American depository receipt (ADR). The company wants to raise capital in the near future through a public offering of the ADR. Which of the following is the most appropriate type of ADR to meet this need?
option_b: Level II
option_c: Level III
explanation_en: Companies can raise money to finance their operations by issuing debt or equity securities. Issuing equity securities gives firms more flexibility since there is no legal obligation to retire equity or distribute dividends to shareholders. Issuing equity securities has several immediate impacts on a company's balance sheet. Common stock, a component of shareholders' equity, increases to account for the value of shares issued. Since cash is an asset, the net proceeds from the offering (ie, the cash received in exchange for the common shares issued) increase total assets. (Choice B) ROE is the ratio of net income to the average book value of common shareholders' equity. Since net income (numerator) is held constant in this case and the issuance of common shares increases the average book value of common shareholders' equity (denominator), ROE decreases. (Choice C) The intrinsic value of a company is the estimated present value of its future cash flows. In this scenario, since everything other than an issuance of common stock is held constant, projected future cash flows would be unchanged, leading to the same intrinsic value for the firm. Since there are more shares outstanding after the new issue, intrinsic value per share would decrease.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best describes a characteristic of common stock?
option_a: It gives the investor an ownership stake in the issuing company.
option_b: It obligates the issuer to repay the amount received from shareholders.
option_c: It does not allow shareholders to participate in the decision-making process.
explanation_en: When investors (usually a group of investors) purchase a controlling share of a company and the company's shares are no longer publicly traded, the company has been taken private. When investors finance that share buyout with a large proportion of debt, it is referred to as a leveraged buyout (LBO). The most attractive candidates for LBOs are companies that have: large amounts of undervalued assets that can be sold to pay down debt and/or high levels of cash flow that can service (ie, pay interest and principal on) the debt (Choices A and B). A high market value relative to book value makes a company potentially less attractive as a buyout target. A high market-to-book (eg, price-to- book value [P/B]) ratio implies that it would be relatively expensive to take a company private since its share price is relatively high, reducing potential returns to the buyout group. Also, a high P/B ratio indicates that the company's assets are less likely to be undervalued.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company uses the proceeds from newly issued bonds to buy back common shares. Holding all else constant, including the common dividend per share, if return on equity increases, the increase is most likely the result of:
option_a: book value of equity declining proportionally more than net income.
option_b: net income increasing due to the increase in tax-deductible interest expense.
option_c: total dividend payments decreasing, resulting in an increase in shareholders' equity.
explanation_en: Types of preference shares (preferred stock) Cumulative Accrues for past dividends that are unpaid Noncumulative Does not accrue dividends that are undeclared and unpaid in past periods Participating Allows for additional dividend payments if company profits exceed a certain threshold Nonparticipating Fixed dividend; no additional payments based on company performance Convertible Can convert into a specified number of common shares Callable Allows issuer to buy back shares from investors for a specified price Putable Allows investors to sell shares back to issuer for a specified price Preferred (preference) shares ownership represents a form of equity investment in a company. Preference shares may grant certain benefits to preferred shareholders such as high dividend payments and in some cases conversion rights (to common stock). Furthermore, dividend payments to preferred shareholders take precedence over dividend payments to common shareholders. Preferred dividends can be cumulative or noncumulative. For cumulative preference dividends, if a company does not pay a dividend (or dividends) in one period (or several periods), the unpaid dividend accrues and is owed in the future. Conversely, for noncumulative preference dividends, the company does not accrue (and does not owe payment for) unpaid dividends from past periods. (Choice A) Unpaid dividends on cumulative preferred shares are accrued and owed to preferred shareholders. (Choice C) Payments of past unpaid dividends are due to preference shareholders before any dividends can be distributed to common shareholders.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Level I sponsored ADRs are most likely:
option_b: used to raise new US equity capital.
option_c: subject to the most stringent SEC filing requirements.
explanation_en: Shareholders often vote in board of director elections, which are conducted via statutory voting or cumulative voting. Often, one vote is tied to each share. In the case of statutory voting, shareholders must allocate their total votes, which are based on the number of open board seats, evenly among the candidates. Under this system, larger shareholders have greater representation than smaller shareholders. In cumulative voting, shareholders can disproportionally allocate their votes to any one candidate (or any number of candidates), which can improve representation for smaller shareholders. In the example above, three board seats are open for election and there are five candidates. Suppose a particular shareholder has 300 votes. Under statutory voting, the shareholder must pick three candidates and distribute 100 votes to each of the three. Under cumulative voting, the shareholder can apply all 300 votes to one candidate. This benefits the shareholder if this shareholder strongly prefers a specific candidate to win a board seat. (Choice A) A cumulative voting system does not change the total number of votes granted to a shareholder. (Choice C) Each vote is cast for one candidate. A single vote cannot be split for multiple candidates.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Which of the following best describes a fundamental difference between preference shares and common shares?
option_a: Preference shares carry more voting rights than common shares.
option_b: Common shares typically have larger dividends than preference shares.
option_c: Preference shareholders receive dividends before common shareholders.
explanation_en: Types of preference shares (preferred stock) Cumulative Accrues for past dividends that are unpaid Noncumulative Does not accrue dividends that are undeclared and unpaid in past periods Participating Allows for additional dividend payments if company profits exceed a certain threshold Nonparticipating Fixed dividend; no additional payments based on company performance Convertible Can convert into a specified number of common shares Callable Allows issuer to buy back shares from investors for a specified price Putable Allows investors to sell shares back to issuer for a specified price Preference (ie, preferred) shares are a type of equity security. Compared to common shares, preference shares often have larger (but fixed) dividends, as well as higher priority over dividend payments and residual claims on a company's assets. There are several types of preference shares (shown in the table above). If preference shares are callable, they have an embedded call option that gives the issuing company (ie, issuer) the right to buy back shares from investors at a predetermined call price. (Choice B) Convertible shares allow shareholders to convert their shares into common stock, not subordinated debt. (Choice C) Participating shares provide shareholders the opportunity to earn additional dividend payments if a company's profits exceed a predetermined threshold. They do not provide voting rights.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\6. Equity Investments\6.04 Overview Of Equity Securities - Answers.pdf
question_en: Holding all other factors constant, an issuance of common stock is most likely to result in an increase to the company's:
option_b: return on equity.
option_c: intrinsic value per share.
explanation_en: Comparison of equity securities Nonconvertible, nonparticipating preferred Common Higher dividend yield Fully participate in company upside Greater downside protection Dividends can increase along with earnings Dividends cannot be increased Dividends cut if earnings fall Limited potential for appreciation Shares can fall to zero if company value declines As owners of a company, common shareholders participate in its operating performance. The more (less) valuable the company becomes, the greater (less) the value of its common shares. Also, common dividends can increase (decrease) with company earnings. Preferred stocks (ie, preference shares) offer advantages relative to common shares. Dividend preference: Preferred dividends must be paid before any common stock dividends can be paid. Asset preference: If the company is liquidated, preferred shareholders must receive the par value of their shares before the common shareholders receive any distributions. However, balancing these preferences are factors that limit the upside for preferred shareholders. Nonparticipating, nonconvertible preferred stocks do not participate in increases in the company's value or in dividend increases due to company performance. To compensate for these limits, preferred stocks usually have greater dividend yields than common stocks. (Choice B) Despite their larger dividend yields compared with common stocks, preferred shares have lower expected returns due to their exclusion from participation in company performance. (Choice C) Due to their seniority and more predictable dividend payments compared to common stock, preferred stocks exhibit lower price volatility.
